meta.title: The Exhaustion of Talking to a Tool
meta.author: ohrv

comments.author: kangalio
comments.text:
Interestingly, for me, talking to AI has become second nature. At this point, I open like 10 chats per day for the most random of queries, and I hardly think about it.

Punch my query in, read it, respond, read it. Like researching via google - which has become as second nature as driving, to the point of the hands being in the flow by themselves. Talking to AI is beginning to grow into just the same niche, at least for me

comments.author: seb
comments.text: I don't think that's a good thing tbh, knowing how prone LLMs are to hallucinating (I remember seeing a study about how like nearly half of all LLM responses aren't accurate, and I doubt that number's improved much (if at all) since then). Depending on how you use them, there's also the risk of deskilling, since you're pretty much offloading your thinking onto them. We should strive to rely less on LLMs, not more.

comments.author: inactive-user
comments.text:
You're probably referring to the BBC study that involved AI queries over their published articles: https://www.bbc.com/mediacentre/2025/bbc-research-shows-issues-with-answers-from-artificial-intelligence-assistants

There was also another survey for Google AI overviews that claimed about 10% of them are incorrect in some way: https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/07/technology/google-ai-overviews-accuracy.html

For what it's worth, I don't think these studies necessarily account for how most people actually use AI tools. I'd characterize most uses as low stakes and not really assignable a truth rating in the first place ("write a polished presentation for my boss", "help me win a Facebook argument", "should I buy Sketchers or Adidas").

I think the main problem with daily use is the sycophancy-fueled positive feedback loop. LLMs will bend over backwards to make you feel smart, and while I'm all for small affirmations every now and then, I think it leads to brain rot when done in excess. I know several folks who are very heavy users, and they might have had small problems before, but they definitely don't seem to be in a healthy place right now.

comments.text:

comments.author: BinaryIgor
comments.text:
I do similarly, but I supplement it more and more with the (brave) search these days; I feel like relying too much on LLMs might atrophy your research skills in the long-run (if overused).

They do too much work of sourcing and compiling knowledge for you; but of course, sometimes you just want to get some low-importance answer and that's completely fine. But in general, I think that our research skills should be kept sharp

comments.author: kprotty
comments.text: I personally havent noticed there being a "research skill" that's lost. It's more so the patience you have to sift through a bunch of noise to find what you want, that atrophies. The ability to concisely locate information or the "unnecessary-filter" itself seems to remain unchanged (once built up / trained)

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text: Evaluating relevance and reliability of contradictory sources is relevant when web-searching on some topics (even with one search engine), but harder to apply in the context of a chatbot which is not outstandingly good at referencing sources for each statement.

comments.author: BinaryIgor
comments.text: ...once built up - yes. The interesting question for a new generation would be: can it be built with access to such advanced tools (LLMs) only? Will see!

comments.author: zem
comments.text: I supplement it because I've had the LLMs tell me something that I go to kagi/google and prove wrong or inadequate within a few minutes (usually I'm told that there is no existing library to do what I want, or the bot recommends a poor library when I am pretty sure a better one exists, and I need to go hunt it down myself)

comments.author: zladuric
comments.text: Yes, the things are correct 85-90% of the time. Which means that if you don't confirm the information, one day a week you're doing incorrect work

comments.author: gspr
comments.text:
I would imagine this work is performed by much the same parts of your brain that are in charge of a conversation with a human being. With the human being, you after a while build up a model of the person's capabilities, strengths and weaknesses, and those help you when interpreting their replies. Are you not worried that you subconsciously attempt to use the same brain regions when "talking" with an AI, and utterly failing at modelling your conversation partner?

Like with so many other ancient human traits, there's ample room for trouble if not paired carefully with modern technology. (Seeking out high-energy foods is a good survival strategy; but one that's perhaps not very smart to leave unchecked in the modern world.)

comments.author: peter-leonov
comments.text:
Same. It's really good at searching for "known" things. It fans out valid queries and filters the "last mile" for me as a personal fully semantic index would do (which Google lacks for cost reasons).

In the past it was bad at researching new terms (like a fresh feature of a language) but now it simply googles in two waives. First to learn about the subject in general and the see step 1.

This "thinking" bit changed a lot for so little. Well done LLM designers, no doubts here.

comments.author: ohrv
comments.text:
Ah I didn't count this in the regular vibecoding workflows. I agree - I open chats to look for some things just like googling and it is pretty lightweight as long as I keep my queries short and don't start doing the extensive back-and-forth.

I also query our codebase when I have specific questions, but that for me is much more like asking a coworker (minus the upsides), because you have to phrase and think and sometimes followup with specifics, and you sometimes get back lies which lead to more rephrasing.

comments.author: zladuric
comments.text:
One of the skills I did lose with LLMs is exactly that careful phrasing.

Up until like a year ago, I would want to ask someone why the function works like this or where do we do that, but then out of respect for their time, I would consider what exactly I want to ask, and rummage around for a bit before hitting send, and by the time I'm ready to send the question, I already know the answer.

... Then sometimes I would still chat with them but I would say something like "hi, how's your day going", or tell them that I wanted to ask them X but I figured it out and I have a dadjoke for them instead or something if the diet.

comments.author: travisgriggs
comments.text:
LLMs ask us to talk to them, but rarely reward that effort in kind.


Speaking of "rewards"... I made an interesting observation about this just a few days ago. I'm working with two fledgling programmers. (For me), this is a tough dance. I just like lifting people up. But when coaching new programmers, I have to critically assess the work they do. So I look for opportunities to build them up with attaboys. WHEN I review work where they've leaned on an LLM, I realized the LLMs have stolen my ability to compliment them and build them up. I can't tell which parts were just generated, and which might have actually been their own step of mastery. So I just end up critiquing the work the LLM has done, and telling them "tell the LLM to do more of/less of". And or them becoming defensive and saying "but the LLM says."

I'm honestly starting to question the value of code reviews. Everybody has their own virtual "coding buddy". And the opportunity to use code reviews as a way to share knowledge seems diminished.

comments.author: gonz
comments.text:
This probably comes off as a bit drastic, but I don't think people being mentored like this should be using LLMs. They're not good for learning in this way and it's likely that your mentees are going to be learning a fraction of what they would if they didn't waste their learning time with an LLM. Using a LLM for bouncing ideas off of, gathering information (and opinions) and then verifying those are all good ways to use LLMs in general, and especially for learners.

What's the actual plan in your workplace? These programmers aren't likely to turn into actual useful programmers in the same way that they would've before LLMs, it's not as if a few years of this type of stuff will actually teach them much except how to prompt more. Does the company want actual programmers or just Claude Operators?

comments.author: travisgriggs
comments.text:
Not sure which of use you are responding to. I'll respond for myself. We're a pretty loose group of a few. We have a lot of autonomy and get pretty close to our customer. What the company wants is to deliver solutions to our end customers that they'll pay us for (or at least derivative, since we really make our money off of hardware; good software helps move the hardware).

Younger engineers with little experience are super spooked by the advent of AI. They are hearing of peers in industry where people are literally being constrained to be only claude operators. Young programmers have always sought to grow skillsets as specific tool operators, because that's what they see in the hiring process. So they understandably want to "learn how to drive claude". They wonder if it will be the thing that is a must have in their next job.

comments.author: gonz
comments.text:
I was asking specifically what the company wants out of training these programmers, I don't expect younger/newer people to have a clue as to what they should do.

Have you considered talking to them about how they're going to have to amass real, retainable and recallable skills themselves in order to be able to actually be useful in operating an LLM beyond just vibecoding? No one is going to pay a decent wage for people who just operate LLMs, and they won't learn what they spend no time doing. What is the plan here, how are these juniors/mids going to actually become useful programmers, dare I say, maybe even useful when there is no Internet connection?

comments.author: wrs
comments.text:
When LLMs are involved it does require a real shift in approach. There are now two levels of review: the actual code change and the way you used the tool to make the change. (I mean, I could always have said you don't know enough vim commands, but this is different…) Both are valid areas of feedback — the difference being there are no experts in the second one yet, so it's more of a collaboration.

That said, the first rule is that if you can't explain the why and what of the change beyond "the LLM says"…rejected, try again.

comments.author: rainbow_bird
comments.text: This is interesting to me because I totally don't think about talking to LLMs like I think about talking to a human. It's a totally different skill. When I'm talking to an LLM I'm trying to elicit a specific response or get it to talk about a specific thing. This means I talk in a very exact way, focusing on precise phrasing and being unambiguous. Talking to a human is different: I still have to be unambiguous, but I also have to be aware that the other person has goals in the conversation that aren't mine, and be constantly listening for questions the other person might ask me to which I need to respond.

comments.author: vivicat
comments.text:
For what it is worth, I don't talk to LLMs at all. My workplace bans them for NDA reasons. Maybe once every other week I need to switch to Google to solve a problem I can't figure out on DuckDuckGo or StackOverflow, and sometimes when I go there I will read an AI overview with a lot of skepticism. But otherwise I just use my brain. It's nice.

I've never had any conversations with ChatGPT or Claude. I played with the OpenAI sandbox briefly before ChatGPT was a thing. I have had a single conversation with Gemini about some coding issue, with me being converted through the Google search. Copilot has never been launched. Nothing else.

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
I think under the author's definition of a tool, Firefox doesn't qualify for me (and on that scale, Chromium is actively malicious and adversarial).

I also have impression that all the menthal-energy-saving/menthal-energy-draining discussions around LLMs are fantastically multi-dimensional.


There is the degree to which people snap to either of human-like chat / no-persistent-mind sides, on top of which introversion/ambiversion/extroversion applies.

There is thinking that is close to linear language or far from linear language — so LLMs are either replacing thinking or the translation from real thinking to annoying human communication practices.

There is «how much faster or slower I can read than I can type» thing


Speaking of social personas and back-and-forth, as articles focuses on. I cannot read humans, I definitely cannot roll back humans, so if I try to get an LLM do something it is very much not like a human conversation. I can look into the pre-reply blabbering and see how ambiguities in my writing have been interpreted! I can keep the beginning of the conversation but rewrite the last request to avoid mistaken interpretations. I can even rewrite the LLM's response in the history if I believe this will guide the later responses.

(I guess hosted LLMs might be less enthusiastic about letting fully rewrite their safety-relevant thinking? Well, yet another reason to only use local models, as if being a hosted oligopoistic service, together with unannounced changes to behaviour, were not enough reasons to avoid hosted hidden-weights LLMs)

Of course all these manipulations would be bad to do on humans even if they were reliable — because humans are long-lived personalities — that's why talking to a tool that is not built to have a persistent mind is sometimes less exhausting. Also the tool won't find it grating if I am too brief and business-like.

And I think the current advice is that rewriting the initial query to avoid a mistake is almost always better than leaving the mistake in the context then clarifying like in a human conversation, no?

comments.text:

comments.author: wrs
comments.text:
There was a good blog post that I can’t find now, where the author talked about exactly this. My paraphrase from memory:

Their whole life they’ve been frustrated by people reading subtextual cues in their speech that they aren’t actually sending. They’re always speaking completely literally, and have mysterious failures in communication because they can’t hear themselves the way a neurotypical person does.

They were hoping LLMs wouldn’t be like that, because they’re computers after all, but to their disappointment it seems the LLMs do the same thing, perhaps because neurotypical folks are doing the RLHF.

One of their examples was Opus cutting corners because it “heard” urgency in the terse instructions the author gave. When they were more verbose, and assured Opus they weren’t in a hurry, it did better.

(edited for clarity)

comments.author: chandlerc
comments.text:
If you ever find the blog post, would be interested.

Generally, what is described is what I somewhat feared. And I can't even imagine how much more exhausting it is to have to mask and synthesize ridiculous (to you) sub textual clues and clarification...

I would really like to see come research into some of the harnesses having built in settings/modes that embed really strong wrapping prompts to aggressively skew the models probabilistic interpretation of the chat prose and the response prose to align more comfortably with different neurodivergences...

comments.author: k749gtnc9l3w
comments.text:
Urgency post https://christophermeiklejohn.com/ai/zabriskie/reliability/2026/04/03/the-feature-that-has-never-worked.html — previously discussed at https://lobste.rs/s/8sqd2j/feature_has_never_worked_broken_auto_live

I think that adding more mixed signals is going to be hard to make reliable, and it needs to be done per-model. I would maybe believe more in a local-sized-LLM finetune accumulating translation-target «personas» that seem to be RLHF targets of various models (probably with different amounts of corporate-speak over time as marketing switches between «you can just ask for features directly!» to higher-ups and damage control after news stories about consequences…).

Precedent-wise, «this is what I really think and amounts of profanities are relevant for relevant level of mess, but please make it a superficially polite business email demanding rectifications from the counterparty» worked well with LLMs years ago, and models seem to pick up pretty coarse signals first, so… might work, actually. (And you can check the rewriting for outright lies just in case)

So basically I don't believe in large corporations caring enough about accessibility to make it safe not to mask, but I can believe in a cheap hack that does the masking for you when the other side doesn't deserve any care.

comments.author: Brids
comments.text: I love talking to Claude, and I’d wager there’s many people the same given they’re trained to be so agreeable to human preferences.

comments.author: andrewballinger
comments.text:
I believe the author is correct, but is using the tool incorrectly.

You don't need to reason back and forth with an LLM when it's going down the wrong track. Having, uncertainty, confusion or debate in the context increases the likelihood of having uncertainty, confusion, and debate farther along.

The most effective technique is to summarize what you know, reframe the problem, and get a new context where you don't go down the blind alley at all.
